title: Kalmijn & Leopold (2019) True/False Quiz
instructions: Choose True or False, then distinguish the first and second parent's deaths, immediate transitions and later changes, and statistical associations and causal interpretations. Percentage descriptions follow the authors' approximate interpretations of their models.

items.prompt: Hypothesis 1, derived from the solidarity perspective, predicts increased contact between siblings after a parent's death.
items.explanation: Parental death may increase siblings' need for mutual support. Hypothesis 1 predicts that this will be reflected in more frequent contact.

items.prompt: The article assumes that the first and second parent's deaths produce effects of identical size and duration on sibling contact.
items.explanation: Hypothesis 2 explicitly predicts a stronger increase after the first parent's death. Visiting and coordinating support for the surviving parent provide additional reasons for siblings to meet.

items.prompt: Hypothesis 4, derived from the kinkeeping perspective, predicts that sibling contact will eventually fall below predeath levels after the second parent's death.
items.explanation: The last parent's death removes an integrative figure connecting the adult children's families. If the network does not fully replace that kinkeeping role, the hypothesis predicts declining contact in the longer term.

items.prompt: The analytic sample contained 3,812 respondents: 1,211 who experienced parental death during observation and 2,601 who did not.
items.explanation: These are the reported event and comparison groups drawn from four waves of the Netherlands Kinship Panel Study. All included respondents had at least one living parent at the first wave.

items.prompt: The findings supported Hypothesis 5, which predicted a short-term increase in sibling conflict after parental death.
items.explanation: The authors found no support for the predicted temporary increase in conflict. This lack of support does not establish that no individual sibling relationship experienced conflict.

items.prompt: Respondents reported both face-to-face contact and conflict for every sibling, so both analyses used the same 10,367 unique sibling dyads.
items.explanation: Contact analyses used 10,367 unique dyads, whereas conflict analyses used 6,186. Conflict questions were limited to at most two siblings, selected randomly when the respondent had more than two.

items.prompt: The article's phone-contact measure includes contact by letters and email as well as telephone.
items.explanation: The second contact item covered the frequency of phone, letter, and email contact over the past 12 months. It was distinct from the face-to-face contact measure.

items.prompt: The fixed effects models use changes over time within observed sibling relationships and include only explanatory variables that vary over time.
items.explanation: The models relate within-relationship changes in contact or conflict to changes in the predictors, removing time-invariant characteristics. Standard errors were adjusted for dyads clustered within families; this design alone does not establish causation.

items.prompt: Because the researchers constructed a person-year file, every respondent was observed once in every year from 2002 through 2015.
items.explanation: The file was an unbalanced panel based on four survey waves, with an average gap of 3.62 years between waves. Years without interviews were omitted; the file did not create annual observations for each respondent.

items.prompt: In the authors' approximate interpretation of the unadjusted model, sibling face-to-face contact increased by about 17% after the first parent's death, with no statistically significant subsequent decline while the second parent remained alive.
items.explanation: The transition coefficient for logged face-to-face contact was about 0.17, which the authors describe as an approximately 17% increase. The duration effect was not statistically significant. These results exclude observations after the second parent's death and do not prove that contact stayed exactly constant.
items.source: Contact after the first parent's death

items.prompt: The authors completely ruled out the possibility that increased sibling contact promoted solidarity with the surviving parent.
items.explanation: They explicitly acknowledged that the direction could run the other way: increased sibling contact might promote solidarity with the surviving parent, rather than only result from it.

items.prompt: Adding contact with and support to the surviving parent reduced the first-parent death coefficient to zero, establishing complete mediation.
items.explanation: The face-to-face coefficient fell from about 0.17 to 0.10, and the phone/letter/email coefficient from about 0.16 to 0.12. The reductions were statistically significant, but positive coefficients remained. This supports the authors' partial-mediation interpretation, not a claim that a complete causal mechanism was established.

items.prompt: The authors describe predicted face-to-face contact about seven years after the second parent's death as approximately 30% below the predeath reference level.
items.explanation: The model showed an initial increase followed by a negative duration pattern. The positive quadratic term indicated that the decline leveled off, but the predicted level remained substantially below the predeath reference. The approximately 30% figure is the authors' model-based description.
items.source: Long-term contact after the second parent's death

items.prompt: Reduced conflict after the second parent's death is direct evidence that sibling relationship quality improved.
items.explanation: Contact declined along with conflict. The authors interpret this combination as relationships fading through reduced interaction, rather than deteriorating through greater conflict; fewer conflicts alone do not demonstrate improved relationship quality.

items.prompt: Although most second-parent deaths were mothers' deaths, the additional analyses found no statistically significant differences by the second parent's gender in the transition or duration effects on face-to-face or phone contact.
items.explanation: In 75% of these cases, the mother died after the father. The absence of significant gender interactions for contact was consistent with an interpretation centered on losing the last parent rather than specifically the mother; it does not prove that gender can never matter.
